short: Nazi Germany successfully launched the V-2, the world's first long-range guided ballistic missile, marking a leap in aerospace technology.
full:
On 3 October 1942, after several failed attempts, engineers at the Peenemünde Army Research Center in Germany successfully launched the Aggregat-4 (A-4) rocket, which would later be known as the V-2 (Vergeltungswaffe 2, or Retaliation Weapon 2). Reaching an altitude of roughly 53 miles (85 kilometres) and travelling 118 miles downrange, it became the first artificial object to reach the fringes of space. Developed under the technical direction of Wernher von Braun, the liquid-propellant rocket represented a staggering technological breakthrough that no Allied power possessed.

Despite its technical sophistication, the V-2 was militarily ineffective and exorbitantly expensive, consuming vast amounts of resources. Its production in the underground Mittelwerk factory relied heavily on forced labour from the Mittelbau-Dora concentration camp, where an estimated 20,000 prisoners died. Following the war, captured V-2 technology and its German engineers formed the foundation of both the American and Soviet space programmes and intercontinental ballistic missile arsenals.
